0.body: This book specifies the language that interrexx implements: the Rexx language as ooRexx extends it. It describes what a program means, and what the interpreter must do when it runs one.
0.title: Introduction

1.body: The book is written for three readers: an engineer changing the interpreter, who needs the exact behavior before touching code; an LLM agent doing the same work, which may read one page at a time with no history behind it; and a reviewer judging whether a change is correct. It assumes you can read Rexx, and it does not teach the language.
1.title: Who it is for

10.body:
Note. Position and length arguments are whole numbers. The two rules below say which strings a whole-number argument accepts and what value it then has. [conv.whole.form] A whole-number argument must be a string of this form: optional whitespace; an optional sign, + or -, which may be followed by whitespace; one or more digits, with at most one period among or around them; optionally an exponent, which is E or e directly after the last digit or the period, an optional sign, and one or more digits; optional whitespace. Any other string raises SYNTAX 40.12, the null string and a string of only whitespace included. say substr('abcdef', ' + 2 ', 1) substr('abcdef', '2.', 1), substr('abcdef', '.2E1', 1) substr('abcdef', '20e-1', 1), substr('abcdef', '2.E0', 1)
signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc', '')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say substr('abc', '1 E1')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say substr('abc', '+-2')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say substr('abc', '0x2')
d: say condition('o')~code b b b b b
40.12
40.12
40.12
40.12 [conv.whole.digits] On a 64-bit host, which is what interrexx targets, the value of a whole-number argument is its number rounded to 18 significant digits; when the first digit dropped is 5 or more, the magnitude rounds up, otherwise down. The caller's NUMERIC DIGITS setting plays no part. If the rounded value has a fractional part other than zero, or its magnitude is 10**18 or more, the argument raises SYNTAX 40.12; otherwise its value is that integer. (The reference manual gives 9 digits for 32-bit hosts; this book does not specify those.) say substr('abcdef', '2.000', 1) substr('abcdef', '1.0000000000000000001', 1)
say '['word('a b', 999999999999999999)']'
numeric digits 3
signal on syntax name a
say substr('abcdef', 2, 1.0001)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say substr('abc', '2.5')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say word('a b', 1000000000000000000)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say word('a b', '999999999999999999.5')
d: say condition('o')~code b a
[]

10.title: Whole-number arguments

11.body:
[conv.method] A builtin that runs as a String method does its work by sending the String message of the same name. One of its arguments, usually the first and for a few builtins the second, is the receiver; the others become the message's arguments, in their order. The builtin and the message then give the same result for the same arguments. A builtin page says when its builtin is one of these. The range checks below, and the order of the checks , are rules for these builtins only; any other builtin's page states its own range checks. say substr('abcd', 2, 2) 'abcd'~substr(2, 2) upper('ab', 2) 'ab'~upper(2) bc bc aB aB Note. The ooRexx reference manual (Functions > Built-in Functions) names the builtins that run this way; the ANSI standard, which has no String methods, does not. [conv.position.check] In a builtin that runs as a String method, a position argument is a whole-number argument whose value must be positive. A value of 0 or less raises SYNTAX 93.924; -0 is 0. signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc', 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say word('a b', '-0')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say substr('abc', -1)
c: say condition('o')~code 93.924
93.924
93.924 [conv.length.check] In a builtin that runs as a String method, a length argument is a whole-number argument whose value must not be negative. A negative value raises SYNTAX 93.923. A length of 0 is allowed, and so is -0, which is 0. say '['substr('abc', 2, 0)']' '['substr('abc', 2, '-0')']'
signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc', 1, -1)
a: say condition('o')~code [] []
93.923 Note. These two codes follow from the reference manual: a builtin of this kind sends a String message, the range of a position or length is checked by that method, and an incorrect call to a method is error 93, whose subcodes 924 and 923 are the position and length cases. The ANSI draft (9.2.1), which has no such methods, raises 40.14 for a position and 40.13 for a length.

12.body:
[conv.pad] A pad argument must be a string of exactly one character. Any character may be the pad, the blank and '00'x included. A pad of any other length raises SYNTAX 40.23; so does the null string, and so does a character that an encoding writes as two bytes ( two characters ). say substr('ab', 1, 4, '*') c2x(substr('ab', 1, 3, '00'x))
signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc', 1, 2, '**')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say substr('abc', 1, 2, '')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say substr('abc', 1, 2, 'c3a9'x)
c: say condition('o')~code ab** 616200
40.23
40.23
40.23
12.title: Pad arguments

13.body:
[conv.arg.omitted] An argument is omitted when its place in the argument list holds no expression: nothing before the first comma, nothing between two commas, or nothing after the last one. An omitted optional argument takes the default that its page states. say substr('abc', 1, , '.') substr('abc', 2, ) abc bc [conv.arg.empty] An argument whose expression yields the null string is not omitted and never takes the default. It is checked like any other value: as a whole number it raises SYNTAX 40.12 ( whole-number form ), as a pad SYNTAX 40.23 ( pad ), and as a string it is the null string. signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc', 1, '')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say substr('abc', 1, 5, '')
b: say condition('o')~code 40.12
40.23
13.title: Omitted and empty arguments

14.body:
[conv.check.order] In a builtin that runs as a String method, when more than one argument fails, the form checks run first: the whole-number checks of form and value , and the pad check, applied to the arguments from left to right, and the first failure is raised. Only when every argument passes them do the range checks of positions and lengths run, again from left to right. A builtin page that has checks of its own states where they fall in this order. signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc', 0, 'x')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say substr('abc', 0, 1, '**')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say substr('abc', 'x', 1, '**')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say translate('abc', , , '**', 'x')
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say substr('abc', 0, -1)
f: say condition('o')~code 40.12
40.23
40.12
40.23
93.924 Note. The range checks come last because they belong to the String method, which runs only once the call has been made. The reference manual does not say that the function call checks the form of its arguments, under error 40, before it sends the message; that part matches ooRexx. The ANSI draft (9.2.1) checks each argument's form and range together, one argument at a time.

15.body:
[conv.error.name] A rule that says something "raises SYNTAX m.n" means that the builtin returns no value and the SYNTAX condition is raised with error number m and subcode n. A trap for it sees condition('C') as SYNTAX, condition('O')~code as the string m.n, and the variable RC set to m. This book does not state the error message. signal on syntax name e
x = substr('abc', 0)
say 'not reached'
e: say condition('c') condition('o')~code rc SYNTAX 93.924 93 [conv.returns] A rule that says a builtin "returns" a string means that the function call's value is exactly that string: the same characters in the same order, with no blanks added or removed. say '['substr('abc', 2)']' '['substr(' a ', 1)']' [bc] [ a ]
15.title: Errors and results

16.body:
[conv.string.deviation.30] interrexx does not convert an argument whose STRING method answers an object that is not a string, such as a Directory. When a builtin receives such an argument where its page calls for a string, interrexx ends the program with exit code 120 and a message that this is not implemented, after raising NOSTRING when a trap for it is set. ooRexx reads the answer as a string, and what it does then depends on the builtin: UPPER ends the program with Error 5, LENGTH answers an unrelated number, and STRIP crashes the interpreter. A program can rely on none of these answers. o = .weird~new
say 'before'
say upper(o)
say 'after'
::class weird
::method string return .directory~new before
16.title: Deviations

17.body:
ANSI: 9.2.1; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions Deviations: D4 This chapter has a page for each builtin function, and each page specifies the function call. The rules here hold for every builtin call; the pages link to them, and to the conventions , instead of restating them. A page's syntax line names the arguments in order. A name in square brackets is an optional argument; every other argument is required. The number of names on the line is the most arguments the builtin takes, and the number of required ones is the fewest. [bif.index.call.count] The argument count of a call is the position of the last argument in it that is not omitted . Omitted places at the end of the list therefore add nothing to the count, and a call with only omitted places counts as a call with no arguments, a count of 0. say substr('abc', 2, , ) word('a b', 2, , , ) bc b [bif.index.call.too-few] A call whose argument count is less than the number of required arguments raises SYNTAX 40.3. signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say substr('abc', )
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say word(, , )
c: say condition('o')~code 40.3
40.3
40.3 [bif.index.call.too-many] A call whose argument count is greater than the number of arguments on the syntax line raises SYNTAX 40.4, whatever the values of the arguments, and even when the arguments before the last are omitted. signal on syntax name a
say word('a b', 1, 2)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say substr(, , , , 1)
b: say condition('o')~code 40.4
40.4 [bif.index.call.missing] A required argument that is omitted, in a call whose argument count reaches past it, raises SYNTAX 40.5. signal on syntax name a
say substr(, 1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say wordpos('a', , 1)
b: say condition('o')~code 40.5
40.5 [bif.index.call.order.count-before-missing] A call whose argument count is wrong raises the too-few or too-many error even when it also omits a required argument . signal on syntax name a
say word(, 1, 2)
a: say condition('o')~code 40.4 [bif.index.call.order.count-before-values] A call whose argument count is wrong raises the too-few or too-many error even when an argument it does pass would fail its own check. signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc', 'x', 1, '**', 5)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say word('a b', 0, 2)
b: say condition('o')~code 40.4
40.4 [bif.index.call.order.missing-before-values] A call whose argument count is right but that omits a required argument raises SYNTAX 40.5 even when an argument it passes after the omitted one would fail its own check, a form check or a range check. signal on syntax name a
say substr(, 'x')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say subword(, 0)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say wordpos(, 'a', 0)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say verify('abc', , 'Y')
d: say condition('o')~code 40.5
40.5
40.5
40.5 Note. The ANSI draft (9.2.1) checks the arguments from left to right, raising 40.5 at an omitted required argument before it reaches the ones after it, and makes the range checks only once every argument is present.
17.title: Built-in functions

18.body:
[bif.index.words.split] The builtins that count words split a string into words the same way. A word is a run of one or more characters, none of them whitespace , that has whitespace or an end of the string on each side. The words of a string are numbered from 1, left to right. Whitespace before the first word, between two words and after the last belongs to no word, so the null string and a string of only whitespace have no words. Every other character, line feed and '00'x among them, can be part of a word. say words(' a'||'09'x||'b c ') words('') words(' '||'09'x)
say word('one two', 2) c2x(word('a'||'0a000c'x||'b c', 1)) 3 0 0
two 610A000C62 Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.26 and the other word builtins) separates words by a set of blank characters that it leaves to the configuration: the blank and any others the configuration names. ooRexx fixes that set as the blank and the horizontal tab, and so does this book. [bif.index.words.number] Where a word builtin's page calls an argument a word number, that argument is a position that counts words: the word number n names word n of the string as the word rule numbers them. A word number greater than the number of words in the string is not an error, for every value that passes its check; it names no word, and the builtin's page says what the builtin answers then. say '['word('a b', 3)']' wordindex('a b', 3) wordlength('a b', 999999999999999999), wordpos('a', 'a b', 3)
signal on syntax name e
say wordindex('a b', 0)
e: say condition('o')~code [] 0 0 0
93.924
18.title: Words

19.body:
[bif.index.count.answer] WORDINDEX, WORDLENGTH, WORDPOS and VERIFY each answer a count: of characters or of words, or a position, which counts characters or words up to the one it names. A builtin that answers a count writes it as a whole number in decimal digits only: no sign, no leading zero, no period and no exponent, and 0 for zero. The caller's NUMERIC DIGITS setting plays no part, so the answer is exact however many digits it has. numeric digits 3
say wordindex(copies(' ', 1000) || 'a', 1) wordlength(copies('z', 1234), 1), wordpos('y', copies('x ', 1200) || 'y') wordpos('q', 'a b')
say verify(copies('a', 1200) || 'b', 'a') verify(copies('a', 1300), '', 'N', 1234), verify('ab', 'ab') 1001 1234 1201 0
1201 1234 0 Note. The reference manual does not say how these answers are written or whether NUMERIC DIGITS applies to them; this rule matches ooRexx. [bif.index.count.answer.deviation.4] interrexx does not specify whether the answer of a builtin that answers a count is the same object as another string of equal value: as an equal number the program already holds, such as the start argument of a call that answers it, or a literal such as '1201', or the equal answer of another call. Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable or IdentitySet, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one. w = copies('x ', 1200) || 'y'
n = 1200 + 1
say (wordpos('y', w, n) == n) (wordindex(copies(' ', 1200) || 'a', 1) == '1201'), (wordlength(copies('z', 1201), 1) == wordpos('y', w))
v = copies('a', 1300)
say (verify(v, '', 'N', n) == n) (verify(copies('a', 1200) || 'b', 'a') == '1201') 1 1 1
1 1

19.title: Answers that are counts

2.body: This book is normative in its own right: its rules define the language interrexx implements, and no other document or implementation does. When the interpreter and a rule disagree, one of them has a defect, and the disagreement is settled here before it is settled in code. Behavior the book does not state is not promised, and where a reader might expect a promise the book says explicitly that a behavior is not specified. Rules and examples are normative. Everything else is informative: the overview at the top of a page, and every note, which is set as a block quote that begins Note. A note explains where a rule comes from or how another definition of Rexx differs; it never adds to or changes a rule.
2.title: Authority

20.body: SUBSTR(string, n [, length] [, pad]) ANSI: 9.3.21; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > SUBSTR (Substring) Deviations: D4 SUBSTR selects a run of characters from a string by position, and pads the run when it reaches past the end of the string.
20.title: SUBSTR

21.body:
[bif.substr.method] SUBSTR is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver. string is a string , n is a position , length is a length , and pad is a pad . The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules : two are required and four is the most. signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc', 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say substr('abc', 2, -1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say substr('abc', 1, 2, '..')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say substr('abc', 1, 1, '.', 1)
d: say condition('o')~code 93.924
93.923
40.23
40.4 [bif.substr.length.default] When length is omitted, it is the number of characters of string at position n and after it: LENGTH(string) - n + 1 when n is at most LENGTH(string), and 0 otherwise. say '['substr('abcde', 2)']' '['substr('abcde', 5)']', '['substr('abcde', 6)']' '['substr('abcde', 100)']' [bcde] [e] [] [] Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.21) computes the omitted length as LENGTH(string) + 1 - n and repeats that many times, so for n two or more past the end its count is negative and its definition raises SYNTAX 26.2 from inside the builtin. This page follows ooRexx, where the reference manual says the rest of the string is returned and positions past the end select nothing, so the result is the null string. [bif.substr.pad.default] When pad is omitted, it is the blank, '20'x. say '['substr('xyz', 3, 3)']' [z ]
21.title: Arguments

22.body:
[bif.substr.result] SUBSTR returns a string of exactly length characters. Its character at position i, for each i from 1 to length, is the character of string at position n + i - 1 when string has a character there, and pad otherwise. So the result is the characters of string from position n on, at most length of them, followed by as many copies of pad as make up the length. say '['substr('abcdef', 2, 3)']' '['substr('abcdef', 4, 5, '.')']', '['substr('abcdef', 1, 6)']' [bcd] [def..] [abcdef] [bif.substr.past-end] When n is greater than LENGTH(string), no character of string is selected: the result is length copies of pad, and the null string when length is omitted. This holds for every n past the end that passes its check. say '['substr('abc', 4, 2, '*')']' '['substr('abc', 999999999999999999, 3, '*')']', '['substr('abc', 4)']' [**] [***] [] [bif.substr.length.zero] When length is 0, the result is the null string, for every n that passes its check. pad is still checked, as a pad always is. say '['substr('abc', 2, 0)']' '['substr('abc', 10, 0, '*')']'
signal on syntax name e
say substr('abc', 2, 0, '')
e: say condition('o')~code [] []
40.23 [bif.substr.empty] When string is the null string, every position is past its end, so the result is length copies of pad, or the null string when length is omitted. say '['substr('', 1)']' '['substr('', 1, 3)']' '['substr('', 5, 2, '-')']' [] [ ] [--] [bif.substr.bytes] SUBSTR selects and pads by character , one byte each, and copies every byte unchanged: whitespace, control characters and '00'x are characters like any other, in string and as pad. say c2x(substr('61000962'x, 2, 4, '00'x)) 00096200
22.title: The result

23.body:
[bif.substr.deviation.4] interrexx does not specify whether the result of SUBSTR is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when the call returns all of it unchanged as substr(s, 1) does, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'abc' beside substr('abcdef', 1, 3). Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable or IdentitySet, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one. s = 'abc' || 'def'
say (substr(s, 1) == s) (substr('abcdef', 1, 3) == 'abc') 1 1
23.title: Deviations

24.body: SUBWORD(string, n [, length]) ANSI: 9.3.22; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > SUBWORD Deviations: D4 SUBWORD selects a run of consecutive words from a string, keeping the whitespace between them as it is. Words are those of the word rule .
24.title: SUBWORD

25.body:
[bif.subword.method] SUBWORD is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver. string is a string , n is a word number , and length is a length that counts words. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules : two are required and three is the most. signal on syntax name a
say subword('a b', 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say subword('a b', 1, -1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say subword('a b', 0, 'x')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say subword('a b', 1, 1, 1)
d: say condition('o')~code 93.924
93.923
40.12
40.4 [bif.subword.length.default] When length is omitted, it selects every word from word n to the last word of string. say '['subword('one two three', 2)']' '['subword('one two three', 3)']' [two three] [three]
25.title: Arguments

26.body:
[bif.subword.result] When string has a word n and length is not 0, SUBWORD returns the part of string that begins with the first character of word n and ends with the last character of word n + length - 1, or of the last word of string when it has fewer words than that. It is a slice of string and nothing is rewritten in it, so a run of blanks or tabs separating two selected words keeps its length and its characters. Since the slice starts and ends on word characters, whitespace before word n, and after the last selected word, falls outside it. The other cases have rules of their own: n past the last word , length 0 and a string with no words . say '['subword('one two three four', 2, 2)']'
say '['subword(' one two ', 1)']' '['subword('a b c', 2, 100)']'
say c2x(subword('09'x||'a'||'0909'x||'b'||'09'x, 1)) [two three]
[one two] [b c]
61090962 [bif.subword.past-end] When n is greater than the number of words in string, the result is the null string. This holds for every n past the last word that passes its check. say '['subword('a b c', 4)']' '['subword('a b c', 999999999999999999, 2)']' [] [] [bif.subword.length.zero] When length is 0, the result is the null string, for every n that passes its check. say '['subword('a b c', 2, 0)']' '['subword('a b c', 9, 0)']' [] [] [bif.subword.empty] When string has no words, the null string or a string of only whitespace among them, the result is the null string for every n and length that pass their checks. say '['subword('', 1)']' '['subword(' '||'09'x||' ', 1, 2)']' [] [] [bif.subword.nonblank] A character that the word rule places inside a word, such as a line feed or a carriage return, is copied into the result as it stands, and SUBWORD ends the result after it when it is the last character of the last selected word. say c2x(subword('a'||'0a'x||'b c', 1, 1)) c2x(subword('a'||'0d'x||' b', 1, 1)) 610A62 610D
26.title: The result

27.body:
[bif.subword.deviation.4] interrexx does not specify whether the result of SUBWORD is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when the call returns all of it unchanged as subword(w, 1) does for a w with no whitespace around its words, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'a b' beside subword('a b c', 1, 2). Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable or IdentitySet, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one. w = 'a' || ' b'
say (subword(w, 1) == w) (subword('a b c', 1, 2) == 'a b') 1 1

28.body: TRANSLATE(string [, tableo] [, tablei] [, pad] [, pos] [, length]) ANSI: 9.3.23; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > TRANSLATE Deviations: D4, D94 TRANSLATE replaces characters of a string, or of a run of its characters, through a pair of tables: a character found in the input table tablei is replaced by the character at the same position in the output table tableo. Called with no table and no pad, it uppercases instead.
28.title: TRANSLATE

29.body:
[bif.translate.method] TRANSLATE is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver; the other five become the message's arguments, in their order. string, tableo and tablei are strings , pad is a pad , pos is a position , and length is a length . The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules : one is required and six is the most. say translate('tab', 'TB', 'tb') 'tab'~translate('TB', 'tb', , 2)
signal on syntax name a
say translate('abc', , , , 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say translate('abc', , , , 1, -3)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say translate('abc', 'x', 'a', '--')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say translate('abc', , , , 'one')
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say translate('abc', , , , 1, 1, 1)
f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
say translate(, 'x')
g: say condition('o')~code TaB taB
93.924
93.923
40.23
40.12

3.body: ooRexx. The open-source C++ implementation of Object Rexx, version 5. interrexx is written to run ooRexx programs, and the book's examples are also run on ooRexx to measure where the two agree. Deviation. A declared difference between interrexx and ooRexx, numbered in the project's register. A page lists in its front matter the deviations that touch its element, and states each as a rule whose identifier ends deviation.N. Every example on which interrexx and ooRexx answer differently belongs to such a rule; any other difference is a defect. String method. A method of the String class. Many builtins run as one, as the conventions define. Identity. Whether two values are the same object, as opposed to equal strings. It is observable only through identityHash and the identity collections (IdentityTable, IdentitySet), and the book says where it is not specified.
3.title: Terms

30.body:
[bif.translate.upper] When tableo, tablei and pad are all omitted, TRANSLATE returns string with each character of the run from pos for length characters uppercased as UPPER does , and every other character unchanged. The result is then UPPER(string, pos, length), with the same defaults for pos and length. say translate('hello, world') translate('hello, world', , , , 8, 3) HELLO, WORLD hello, WORld [bif.translate.result] When at least one of tableo, tablei and pad is given, TRANSLATE returns a string of LENGTH(string) characters. Each character c of string at a position from pos to pos + length - 1 is looked up in tablei. When c occurs in it, let k be the position of its first occurrence: the result has, in place of c, the character of tableo at position k when LENGTH(tableo) is at least k, and pad otherwise. When c does not occur in tablei, it is copied unchanged, and so is every character of string outside the run. say translate('a1b2c3', 'xyz', 'abc') translate('a1b2c3', 'xyz', '123', , 3) x1y2z3 a1bycz [bif.translate.first] When a character occurs more than once in tablei, its first occurrence alone decides what it becomes; the characters of tableo at the positions of the later occurrences are never used. say translate('mom', 'abc', 'mmo') translate('mom', '123', 'omo') aca 212 [bif.translate.tableo.length] tableo need not be as long as tablei. When it is shorter, a character found in tablei at a position past the end of tableo is replaced by pad; when it is longer, its characters past the length of tablei are never used. say translate('wxyz', 'WX', 'wxyz', '+') translate('wxyz', 'WXYZ123', 'wx') WX++ WXyz [bif.translate.pad-only] When both tables are omitted and pad is given, every character of the run is replaced by pad, since every character is found in the default tablei and the default tableo has no characters. say translate('secret', , , '*') translate('secret', , , '*', 3, 2) ****** se**et Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.23) uppercases whenever both tables are omitted and ignores pad then. This page follows ooRexx, where the reference manual says a given pad replaces the whole string. [bif.translate.tablei.empty] When tablei is given as the null string, no character is found in it, and the result is string unchanged, for every tableo, pad, pos and length that pass their checks. say translate('abc', 'xyz', '') translate('abc', , '', '*') translate('abc', '', '') abc abc abc Note. This holds however the null string was produced, which ooRexx does not do: see Deviation 94 . 4.body: Every statement the book makes about behavior is a rule. A rule has an identifier of dotted lowercase words, and it is a single short paragraph. An identifier names the page that holds its rule, so a reader of the raw Markdown finds any rule from its identifier alone. The first word names the chapter: bif for built-in functions in builtins/, instr for instructions/, expr for expressions/, parse for parsing/, cond for conditions/ and class for classes/. The second word is the page's file name: bif.substr.pad is in builtins/substr.md, and the rules for a whole chapter, such as bif.index.call.count, are in its index.md. The conventions are one page, conventions.md, and every conv. rule is there. The checker rejects a rule on any other page. Identifiers never change and are never reused. Other pages refer to a rule by that identifier, and so do comments in the test sources: a test that exercises a rule cites it, and the checker reports any rule that has neither a cited test nor an example.

[bif.wordpos.result] When phrase has at least one word, let m be the number of its words. WORDPOS then returns the smallest word number k, with k at least start, such that string has a word k + m - 1 and, for each i from 1 to m, word k + i - 1 of string is equal under == to word i of phrase. When there is no such k, the result is 0. A phrase with no words is the case of its own rule . The answer is written as a count , and whether it is a new object is not specified . s = 'one two three two three four'
say wordpos('two', s) wordpos('two three', s) wordpos('two three', s, 3), wordpos('two three', s, 5) wordpos(s, s) 2 2 4 0 1 [bif.wordpos.whitespace] Only the words of phrase and of string take part in the search. The whitespace before the first word, between two words and after the last, in either argument, plays no part: neither how long a run of it is nor whether it is blanks or tabs changes the answer. s = 'one two three two three four'
say wordpos('two' || '09'x || ' three', s) wordpos(' two three ', s), wordpos('two three', 'one two' || '0909'x || 'three') 2 2 2 [bif.wordpos.exact] Two words are equal only when they have the same characters in the same order. Case matters, no numeric comparison is made, and a word of phrase never matches only a part of a word of string. A character that the word rule places inside a word, such as a line feed, must match like any other. s = 'one two three two three four'
say wordpos('Two', s) wordpos('tw', s) wordpos('wo', s) wordpos('two thr', s)
say wordpos('1', '01 1.0 1') wordpos('a b', 'a' || '0a'x || 'b'), wordpos('a' || '0a'x || 'b', 'a b a' || '0a'x || 'b') 0 0 0 0
3 0 3 [bif.wordpos.overlap] Every word number from start on is a candidate for k, including a word inside an earlier candidate that matched in part. A partial match does not make the search skip past the words it covered, so a sequence found can overlap one that was tried before it. say wordpos('a a', 'a a a', 2) wordpos('a b a', 'a b a b a', 2), wordpos('a a b', 'a a a b') 2 3 2 [bif.wordpos.partial] A sequence must lie wholly within string. When the words of phrase match the last words of string but phrase has more words after them, the phrase is not found there, and the result is 0 unless it is found earlier. s = 'one two three two three four'
say wordpos('four five', s) wordpos('three four five', s) wordpos('x y', 'x') 0 0 0 [bif.wordpos.past-end] When start is greater than the number of words in string, the result is 0, for every start that passes its check. A start equal to the number of words searches the last word alone. s = 'one two three two three four'
say wordpos('four', s, 6) wordpos('four', s, 7) wordpos('one', s, 999999999999999999) 6 0 0 [bif.wordpos.empty-phrase] When phrase has no words, the null string or a string of only whitespace among them, the result is 0 for every string, the null string included. start is still checked, as a word number always is. say wordpos('', 'a b') wordpos(' ' || '09'x, 'a b') wordpos('', '')
signal on syntax name e
say wordpos('', '', 0)
e: say condition('o')~code 0 0 0
93.924 [bif.wordpos.empty-string] When string has no words, the result is 0 for every phrase and every start that passes its check. say wordpos('a', '') wordpos('a', ' ' || '09'x, 1) 0 0 Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.28) defines WORDPOS by comparing the phrase, with its whitespace reduced to single blanks, against each run of the same number of words of the string, reduced the same way, from start on. That gives the answers above.
51.title: The result

6.body: Two documents are cited by section and are not copied: the ooRexx reference manual and the ANSI Rexx standard (X3.274-1996, cited from its final public draft, so the notes call it the ANSI draft). A page's front matter names the sections that describe its element. Both are informative: the rules are derived from them and from reasoning about the semantics, and where the two disagree the rule follows ooRexx and a note says how ANSI differs. Where both are silent, a rule matches ooRexx, and a note says so. The wording of this book is its own.
6.title: Sources

7.body: ANSI: 9.2.1; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions Deviations: D30 The rules on this page hold on every page that links to them. A builtin page states what its arguments are (a string, a position, a length, a pad) and links here for what that means, instead of restating it.
7.title: Conventions

8.body:
[conv.string.chars] A string is a finite sequence of characters, and a character is one byte: any of the 256 values from '00'x to 'FF'x. The length of a string is the number of bytes in it. No rule in this book decodes a string in UTF-8 or any other encoding, so a character that such an encoding writes as two bytes is two characters here. say length('c3a9'x)
say c2x(substr('c3a9'x, 2)) 2
A9 [conv.string.null] The null string is the string of length 0, written ''. A builtin makes no check of an argument its page calls a string: no string there raises an error, so the null string and a string of any bytes are as valid as any other. say length(upper(''))
say c2x(upper('61007a'x)) 0
41005A [conv.string.object] An argument that a page calls a string and that is an object other than a string is replaced by the answer of its STRING method, and the builtin works on that answer. When the answer is not a string either, see Deviation 30 . say upper(.object~new) length(.array~of(1, 2)) AN OBJECT 3 [conv.string.whitespace] Whitespace is the blank, '20'x, and the horizontal tab, '09'x, and no other character. Line feed, carriage return, form feed and vertical tab are not whitespace. signal on syntax name e
say substr('abc', '09'x || '2 ')
say substr('abc', '2' || '0a'x)
e: say condition('o')~code bc
40.12
8.title: Strings and characters

9.body:
[conv.position.origin] Positions count from 1. Position 1 is the first character of a string, or its first word where a page counts words, position 2 the one after it, and so on. No character or word is at position 0. say substr('abc', 1, 1) substr('abc', 3, 1)
say word('x y z', 2) a c
y
